summary:
Cyprus does not criminalise same-sex sexual activity. Consensual conduct was decriminalised in 1998, when the European Court of Human Rights held in Modinos v. Cyprus that Criminal Code section 171 violated the right to private life. The offence of promoting homosexuality was lifted in 2000 and unequal ages of consent were equalised in 2002; the universal age of consent is 17. The former military exclusion of homosexuals, which rested on treating homosexuality as a mental illness, has been removed. In the northern part of the island, deputies voted on 27 January 2014 to repeal the provision that punished homosexual acts with up to five years' imprisonment.

Cypriot law provides no general prohibition of discrimination based on gender identity. The 2004 Equal Treatment in Employment and Occupation Law, adopted to transpose the EU Employment Framework Directive of 2000, prohibits sexual-orientation discrimination in employment only, and gender identity is not among its enumerated grounds. Coverage of sexual orientation and gender identity is reported for 2017 in social protection, social insurance, social benefits, health care, education, participation in unions and professional organisations, and access to goods and services, but an LGBTI NGO assessed the resulting framework as fragmented and inadequate, and housing benefits were found to favour "traditional" families. The European Commission's network of legal experts has reported on the transposition of EU equality rules into Cypriot law in 2020 and again in 2024.

Article 99 of the Penal Code, headed "Incitement to violence or hatred due to sexual orientation or gender identity", punishes intentional public threatening, insulting or offensive urging or incitement, spoken or written, of violence or hatred on those grounds with imprisonment of up to three years or a fine. Parliament raised the fine from €5,000 to €10,000 in October 2024. Law 87(I)/2015 criminalises public incitement to violence or hatred on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, and Law 31(I)/2017 makes prejudice motivation an aggravating factor in sentencing. The hate-speech offence dates to a 2013 penal code amendment that carried up to three years' imprisonment and a €5,000 fine.

Conversion practices were criminalised by a House Plenum vote on 25 May 2023, under Law 39(I)/2023, which bans and criminalises the practice.

No gender-recognition law is in force. A bill drafted with the support of the President and the Justice Minister, following a November 2017 meeting between President Nicos Anastasiades and Accept-LGBT Cyprus, would allow persons over 18 to change legal gender on the basis of self-determination, without diagnosis, hormonal treatment or sex reassignment surgery. The Council of Ministers approved the bill in September 2022 and it received a first parliamentary reading in November 2022; it remained pending in 2024. In June 2019 four parents of transgender children publicly urged its speedy adoption after months of delay. At the 2019 Universal Periodic Review the national report stated that legislation for correcting registered sex, for adults and minors, was in preparation and would require only a decision of the Registrar, with no prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports. Queer Cyprus's guidance describes the recognition model it advocates as self-determination without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping, and records that the northern part of the island operates its own recognition process, which explicitly includes non-binary identities.

Marriage is legally recognised only as a union between one man and one woman, and no same-sex marriage is recognised. A civil-union law passed on 26 November 2015 by 39 votes to 12 with 3 abstentions and took effect on 9 December 2015, granting several marriage rights and benefits to both same-sex and opposite-sex partners under statutory legislation termed "civil unions". It does not extend to adoption, which remains reserved to heterosexual couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status can register a civil union but cannot jointly adopt.

Enforcement of the hate-speech and hate-crime provisions is inconsistent. Incitement against LGBT people has in some cases drawn no police or legal action, most visibly when committed by clergy of the Greek Orthodox Church. In a February 2019 attack on a gay man in Nicosia police failed to establish a hate-crime motive, and a second Nicosia incident four months later drew no police action. Eleven complaints were examined in 2015 and five criminal prosecutions were pending trial.

Cyprus accepted all the SOGIESC recommendations it received at its 2019 Universal Periodic Review, which covered combating discrimination and violence, criminalising harassment, adopting an action plan against homophobia and transphobia, and adopting a gender-recognition law. No anti-homophobia action plan exists. ECRI has urged that gender identity be added as a prohibited ground of discrimination.
tangentialFactors:
The island is divided administratively, and the northern part runs its own legal and recognition arrangements. Deputies there voted on 27 January 2014 to repeal the provision punishing homosexual acts with up to five years' imprisonment, and its gender-recognition process explicitly includes non-binary identities.

Cyprus is an EU member state, so EU equality directives and the European Commission's network of legal experts shape the national framework; the Commission's country reports on non-discrimination (2020) and on gender equality (2024) document the transposition.

Cyprus joined the Equal Rights Coalition in August 2018 as its 40th member, and its 2019 Universal Periodic Review produced SOGIESC recommendations that the state accepted in full.
localsOnly:
The Ministry of Education established the programme "HOMBAT - Combating Homophobic and Transphobic Bullying at Schools" in 2017 to train and sensitise teachers and professors on bullying and harassment directed at LGBT students.

Prison guards received two days of LGBTI+ training in April 2023, after anti-LGBTI harassment complaints were made to the Ombudswoman.

Queer Cyprus operates a confidential psychosocial and legal support line seven days a week, covering identity, work, family, shelter, health and military-service issues.

Many LGBTI people in Cyprus are not open about their sexual orientation or gender identity and do not report homophobic violence or discrimination.
outOfScopeNotes:
The number of SOGIESC recommendations accepted at the 2019 Universal Periodic Review is recorded as eight by ILGA and as seven in other accounts; the discrepancy is unresolved.

The Queer Cyprus booklet describes a self-determination recognition framework without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping while no gender-recognition law is in force; whether it describes current practice in the northern part of the island, the model advocated for the Republic of Cyprus, or both, is not resolved by the sources.

The status of the gender-recognition bill after 2024 is not sourced.

A 2017 account of incitement provisions carrying up to five years' imprisonment and a €10,000 fine sits against Article 99's three-year maximum; the relationship between the two is not explained in the sources.

The 2017 claim that antidiscrimination coverage extends to gender identity across several fields is not reconciled in the sources with the equal-treatment law's grounds, which do not include gender identity.

The 2015 complaint and prosecution figures are not dated as to the reporting year.
